prompt: Which of the following best states the central limitation of GDP as a measure of economic performance?

options.label: A
options.text: Useful only for economies of equal size

options.label: B
options.text: Measures output while omitting dimensions of well-being

options.label: C
options.text: Too easy to calculate accurately

options.label: D
options.text: Overcounts output by including government purchases

options.label: E
options.text: Provides no useful information about economic production

explanation: states that GDP is a useful - not useless - indicator of economic performance, but it has limitations. The most fundamental is that it omits nonmarket transactions (unpaid work, volunteer activity, subsistence production) and fails to capture many dimensions of well-being such as income distribution, environmental quality, and leisure.

prompt: A "nonmarket transaction" is best defined as an economic activity that

options.label: A
options.text: Involves illegal goods concealed from tax authorities

options.label: B
options.text: Occurs between businesses rather than involving consumers

options.label: C
options.text: Uses barter and therefore has zero production value

options.label: D
options.text: Occurs abroad rather than within domestic borders

options.label: E
options.text: Provides value without a recorded market exchange

explanation: A nonmarket transaction produces real economic value - such as a parent caring for their own child or a homeowner painting their own house - but because no market price is recorded, it is not captured in GDP. This is one of the primary limitations of GDP as a welfare measure.

prompt: A parent spends 20 hours per week providing unpaid childcare for their own child. This activity

options.label: A
options.text: Included as government transfer payments

options.label: B
options.text: Subtracted as lost paid-labor-market output

options.label: C
options.text: Included only when the parent is unemployed

options.label: D
options.text: Excluded as unpaid household services

options.label: E
options.text: Included as valuable household services

explanation: Unpaid household childcare is a nonmarket transaction. Even though the service has real value - equivalent to what a paid childcare worker would provide - it is excluded from GDP because no market price is observed; this causes GDP to understate the true value of production in the economy.

prompt: A homeowner mows her own lawn rather than hiring a landscaping service. How does this activity affect the accuracy of GDP as a welfare measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Unpaid landscaping adds value without a market transaction

options.label: B
options.text: Unpaid household production is too small to matter

options.label: C
options.text: The homeowner's unpaid time is counted as income

options.label: D
options.text: Saved money is directly included in household output

options.label: E
options.text: The lawnmower is classified as business investment

explanation: When the homeowner hires a landscaper, that transaction is recorded in GDP (as consumer spending on services). When she mows her own lawn, the same service is produced but not counted - it is a nonmarket activity; this means GDP systematically understates the value of self-produced household services, a key limitation.

prompt: Which of the following is an example of a nonmarket transaction excluded from GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: Paying a contractor to repave a public road

options.label: B
options.text: Paying $40 for a salon haircut

options.label: C
options.text: Providing unpaid services at a food bank

options.label: D
options.text: Selling newly baked bread to final consumers

options.label: E
options.text: Selling subscriptions to a newly developed app

explanation: Volunteer work (unpaid labor) is a nonmarket transaction; the food bank volunteer produces real value - meals, services, community support - but because no wage is paid and no price is recorded, this activity is excluded from GDP.

prompt: GDP does NOT directly measure which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Income earned by factors of production

options.label: B
options.text: Income distribution among households

options.label: C
options.text: Value of final domestic goods and services

options.label: D
options.text: Government purchases of goods and services

options.label: E
options.text: New business investment in capital equipment

explanation: GDP measures total output and total income, but it does not reveal how that income is distributed among households. Two countries can have the same GDP per capita while one has extreme inequality and the other has relatively equal distribution; income distribution is a major dimension of well-being that GDP ignores.

prompt: Two countries each have a GDP of $500 billion. Country A has 10 million people; Country B has 100 million people. Why does this comparison illustrate a limitation of GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: Population matters only when income distributions differ

options.label: B
options.text: Different currencies always prevent valid GDP comparisons

options.label: C
options.text: Larger population necessarily means lower total welfare

options.label: D
options.text: Identical total GDP makes every comparison meaningless

options.label: E
options.text: Per-person output is $50,000 in A versus $5,000 in B

explanation: Total GDP alone is a poor measure of average living standards when countries differ in population size. GDP per capita (GDP ÷ population) adjusts for population and provides a better indicator of the average economic output available per person; country A: $500B ÷ 10M = $50,000 per capita; Country B: $500B ÷ 100M = $5,000 per capita - a tenfold difference.

prompt: The underground economy refers to

options.label: A
options.text: Activity concealed from authorities and difficult to record

options.label: B
options.text: Production in offshore drilling and ocean industries

options.label: C
options.text: Production occurring outside major urban population centers

options.label: D
options.text: Secret defense purchases recorded in government budgets

options.label: E
options.text: Production in mines and other underground facilities

explanation: The underground (or shadow) economy includes transactions that go unreported - either legal informal activity (e.g., a plumber paid cash who doesn't report it) or outright illegal activity (e.g., drug sales). Because these transactions are not observed or recorded, they are excluded from official GDP, causing GDP to understate actual economic activity.

prompt: A plumber fixes pipes for a neighbor and is paid $300 in cash, which neither party reports to tax authorities. How does this affect GDP measurement?

options.label: A
options.text: Missing records can cause measured production to be understated

options.label: B
options.text: No effect because only market transactions count

options.label: C
options.text: No distortion because the payment offsets the service

options.label: D
options.text: Exactly $300 subtracted because income is unreported

options.label: E
options.text: Exactly $300 added despite missing production records

explanation: This is an underground (informal) economy transaction. A real service ($300 of plumbing) was produced and sold, but because neither party reports it, it is not captured in official GDP figures; this causes GDP to understate actual economic activity - one of its key limitations.

prompt: Which of the following best describes why GDP growth may NOT necessarily mean that citizens' well-being has improved?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater production necessarily reduces overall economic welfare

options.label: B
options.text: Output growth improves welfare only above population growth

options.label: C
options.text: More output necessarily raises income for everyone

options.label: D
options.text: Output growth necessarily reduces real purchasing power

options.label: E
options.text: Inequality, pollution, or lost leisure can offset output gains

explanation: GDP measures the quantity of market output but not the quality, distribution, or sustainability of that output. Growth in GDP can coexist with worsening environmental conditions, rising inequality, declining leisure, or increases in harmful goods - all of which reduce well-being despite higher GDP; this multi-dimensional limitation is central to Topic 2.2.

prompt: Forest fires destroy wilderness, and domestic cleanup and firefighting services cost $2 billion. Holding other production fixed, how does GDP record these services and the environmental damage?

options.label: A
options.text: GDP remains unchanged because damage is excluded

options.label: B
options.text: Cleanup adds $2B; environmental damage is not directly deducted

options.label: C
options.text: GDP falls $2B from lost natural resources

options.label: D
options.text: GDP falls $2B from government borrowing costs

options.label: E
options.text: GDP rises $2B, proving productive capacity improved

explanation: Domestic cleanup and firefighting services add $2 billion to GDP. Destruction of environmental assets is not directly deducted from GDP. A disaster can also reduce other current production; therefore cleanup spending alone does not determine the change in total GDP or national wealth.

prompt: A country dramatically increases its production of tobacco products, boosting GDP by $50 billion. Which limitation of GDP does this scenario illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: GDP counts output without directly measuring welfare effects

options.label: B
options.text: Tobacco is illegal, so output is understated

options.label: C
options.text: Tobacco is intermediate, so output is overstated

options.label: D
options.text: Income accounting necessarily gives a different total

options.label: E
options.text: Tobacco tax revenue is excluded from national output

explanation: GDP adds up all legally produced final goods at market prices without judging whether they improve or harm well-being. A $50B increase in tobacco production raises GDP just as much as $50B of medicine or education; this limitation - that GDP ignores the composition (type) of output - means GDP growth can occur even when the goods being produced are harmful.

prompt: Which paid activity can raise GDP in response to worsening social conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Unpaid help with a neighbor’s housework

options.label: B
options.text: Paid security services prompted by increased crime

options.label: C
options.text: Unpaid tutoring by a parent

options.label: D
options.text: Unpaid household cooking and cleaning

options.label: E
options.text: Unpaid volunteer work at a shelter

explanation: Spending on security systems and private security guards is a market transaction (counted in GDP as consumer spending or business investment), but it represents a defensive expenditure that arises because of a social problem (crime). Higher crime forces households and firms to spend more on protection, raising GDP, but this does not improve - and may reflect a decline in - well-being; GDP counts this spending without subtracting the cost of the crime that caused it.

prompt: Leisure time — the time people spend on recreation, rest, and personal activities outside of paid work — is

options.label: A
options.text: Counted directly as household consumption

options.label: B
options.text: Excluded directly despite contributing to well-being

options.label: C
options.text: Included directly through retirement transfer payments

options.label: D
options.text: Counted directly as imputed unpaid wages

options.label: E
options.text: Subtracted directly as lost productive capacity

explanation: Leisure time is highly valuable to individuals - it contributes directly to well-being - but is not captured in GDP, which only counts market output. If a country's workers collectively reduce their work hours to enjoy more leisure, GDP falls (less output produced) even though citizens may be better off; this makes GDP an incomplete measure of well-being.

prompt: In a country whose statisticians cannot reliably record household food production, subsistence farming is likely to be

options.label: A
options.text: Counted twice because households produce and consume it

options.label: B
options.text: Recorded exclusively as government purchases

options.label: C
options.text: Fully captured without needing production estimates

options.label: D
options.text: Excluded only when the crops are illegal

options.label: E
options.text: Underestimated when production records are missing

explanation: Production of goods for own use is within the national-accounts production boundary and can be estimated. The practical limitation is incomplete measurement, particularly where reliable records are unavailable. Unpaid household services are generally excluded; own-use goods should not be treated as automatically excluded.

prompt: Environmental degradation caused by industrial production

options.label: A
options.text: Subtracted directly from expenditure GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Necessarily lowers GDP by the full pollution cost

options.label: C
options.text: Added directly as a welfare benefit

options.label: D
options.text: Subtracted directly through negative-externality accounting

options.label: E
options.text: Not directly deducted despite its welfare costs

explanation: GDP counts the output of factories without subtracting the environmental damage they cause. A factory that produces $10M of goods and creates $3M of pollution damage adds $10M to GDP - not $7M; the net welfare impact ($7M after environmental cost) is not captured; environmental quality is a dimension of well-being that GDP systematically ignores.

prompt: Country A and Country B both have a GDP per capita of $30,000. In Country A, the wealthiest 10% earn 70% of total income. In Country B, income is relatively equally distributed. What limitation of GDP does this illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Per-capita GDP fails only because prices change

options.label: B
options.text: Equal averages can conceal different income distributions

options.label: C
options.text: Equal distribution necessarily lowers overall economic welfare

options.label: D
options.text: Total GDP must be excluded from per-capita calculations

options.label: E
options.text: Different distributions matter only with identical currencies

explanation: GDP per capita reports an average, which can be highly misleading when income is unequally distributed. If a small fraction of the population earns most of the income, most citizens live well below the average - yet the average GDP per capita looks healthy; this is a fundamental limitation: GDP (and GDP per capita) says nothing about how economic output is distributed.

prompt: Which of the following is a correct statement about GDP as a measure of a nation's economic performance?

options.label: A
options.text: Useful only for large, advanced economies

options.label: B
options.text: Always overstates welfare by counting government purchases

options.label: C
options.text: Useful for output comparisons, incomplete for welfare

options.label: D
options.text: A complete measure of output and welfare

options.label: E
options.text: A complete welfare measure after inflation adjustment

explanation: GDP is a genuinely useful and widely used measure of market output and economic activity over time. However, its limitations - nonmarket transactions, underground economy, income distribution, environmental degradation, leisure, composition of output - mean it is an incomplete measure of overall well-being; this nuanced view (useful but limited) is exactly what MEA-1.B.1 requires.

prompt: When a family hires a professional cleaner to clean their home, the transaction is counted in GDP. When a family member cleans the home themselves, it is not counted in GDP. This inconsistency reflects which limitation of GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: GDP excludes all publicly provided cleaning services

options.label: B
options.text: GDP excludes paid cleaners because wages are low

options.label: C
options.text: GDP counts each paid cleaning service twice

options.label: D
options.text: Paid cleaning is counted; equivalent unpaid services are excluded

options.label: E
options.text: GDP cannot adjust for differences in cleaning quality

explanation: This scenario - often called the "housekeeper" or "nanny paradox" - illustrates how GDP depends on whether production passes through a market. If a parent quits work to care for their children and clean their own house, GDP falls even though the same real services are being provided; the market/nonmarket boundary creates an arbitrary distinction that can distort GDP as a welfare measure.

prompt: A country experiences rapid GDP growth driven by a massive increase in arms production. A critic argues that this growth does not necessarily indicate improved living standards. This critique reflects which limitation of GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: Military production is excluded as intermediate output

options.label: B
options.text: Defense spending is excluded from government purchases

options.label: C
options.text: Military purchases necessarily reduce measured total GDP

options.label: D
options.text: Exports are excluded because buyers reside abroad

options.label: E
options.text: GDP counts output without measuring civilian welfare gains

explanation: GDP treats a dollar of arms spending identically to a dollar of healthcare or education spending. An economy could grow rapidly by producing weapons for conflict without any improvement in the daily lives of its citizens; GDP's inability to distinguish between the types of goods produced - its indifference to composition - is a key limitation when using it to assess living standards.

prompt: Which of the following activities would be counted in GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: Unpaid help repairing a neighbor’s fence

options.label: B
options.text: Unpaid musicians performing a free concert

options.label: C
options.text: Unpaid painting of one’s own home

options.label: D
options.text: Paid meals prepared by a restaurant chef

options.label: E
options.text: Unpaid cooking for one’s own household

explanation: The restaurant's paid service to customers is a market transaction - the chef receives a wage (counted in the income approach), and the customers pay for meals (counted as consumer spending in the expenditure approach).

prompt: When economists say that GDP fails to capture "quality of life," they mean that GDP does not measure

options.label: A
options.text: Total income generated by current domestic production

options.label: B
options.text: Health, safety, freedom, and environmental quality

options.label: C
options.text: Inflation-adjusted value of goods and services

options.label: D
options.text: The quantity of goods and services produced

options.label: E
options.text: Market prices of goods and services

explanation: Quality of life encompasses many dimensions - health, education, freedom, safety, environmental quality, social connections - that are not bought and sold in markets and thus are not captured in GDP. A country can have high GDP while also having poor health outcomes, low political freedom, or severe environmental pollution; GDP is an incomplete proxy for quality of life.

prompt: An oil spill damages a fishing industry and coastal ecosystems. Domestic cleanup services cost $1.5 billion. How does GDP directly record the cleanup services and the loss of environmental assets?

options.label: A
options.text: Cleanup adds $1.5B without directly deducting environmental damage

options.label: B
options.text: The spill necessarily reduces total GDP by $1.5B

options.label: C
options.text: Cleanup spending proves overall welfare improved $1.5B

options.label: D
options.text: Environmental damage directly cancels all cleanup spending

options.label: E
options.text: GDP directly deducts $1.5B in environmental damage

explanation: Domestic cleanup services add $1.5 billion to GDP, while environmental asset losses are not directly deducted. Any reduction in current fishing output does lower GDP. Cleanup spending therefore does not establish that total GDP or welfare increased.

prompt: Which of the following statements about GDP per capita is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Per-capita GDP automatically adjusts for price inflation

options.label: B
options.text: Per-capita GDP makes total GDP completely unnecessary

options.label: C
options.text: Per-capita GDP has no use in domestic policy

options.label: D
options.text: Population adjustment removes all GDP welfare limitations

options.label: E
options.text: Output per person omits distribution and environmental quality

explanation: GDP per capita (GDP ÷ population) corrects for population size, making it a more useful cross-country comparison than total GDP. However, it is still an average that masks inequality - and it inherits all of GDP's other limitations (nonmarket transactions, environmental damage, composition, quality of life); it improves on total GDP but does not eliminate its limitations.

prompt: Which group's economic contributions is MOST likely to be understated by GDP in a developing economy with a large rural subsistence sector?

options.label: A
options.text: Domestic foreign-owned firms with recorded production

options.label: B
options.text: Government workers with publicly recorded salaries

options.label: C
options.text: Rural producers with unrecorded subsistence and informal activity

options.label: D
options.text: Export manufacturers with recorded market sales

options.label: E
options.text: Urban factory workers with reported wages

explanation: Rural subsistence farmers produce real output - food that feeds families - but because they do not sell it in formal markets, it is largely excluded from GDP. This causes GDP to substantially understate living standards in economies where subsistence agriculture is widespread, making international comparisons of GDP misleading when they involve countries with large informal rural sectors.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of GDP as a measure of economic well-being?

options.label: A
options.text: Does not directly value leisure time

options.label: B
options.text: Does not directly deduct resource depletion

options.label: C
options.text: Excludes unpaid housework and volunteer services

options.label: D
options.text: Measures current final domestic production

options.label: E
options.text: Does not reveal how income is distributed

explanation: GDP is designed to measure the total market value of final goods and services; this is what it does well.

prompt: A country with a rapidly growing GDP has simultaneously experienced rising pollution levels, increasing income inequality, and a decline in average leisure time. Based on these trends, which of the following conclusions is most warranted?

options.label: A
options.text: Pollution levels alone should replace every output indicator

options.label: B
options.text: Citizens are certainly worse off because pollution increased

options.label: C
options.text: Citizens are certainly better off because output increased

options.label: D
options.text: Welfare costs can offset the benefits of higher output

options.label: E
options.text: Greater inequality is required for output to improve welfare

explanation: Higher GDP is associated with more market output, but the accompanying environmental degradation, increased inequality, and loss of leisure all reduce aspects of well-being that GDP does not measure. The most accurate conclusion is that GDP growth overstates the improvement in overall welfare when these negative dimensions are excluded from the calculation.

prompt: Two economists debate whether GDP is a good measure of a nation's well-being. Which position is most consistent with the AP Macroeconomics curriculum?

options.label: A
options.text: An output indicator excluding all government production

options.label: B
options.text: An inflation indicator providing no information about output

options.label: C
options.text: A useless indicator that should always be abandoned

options.label: D
options.text: A useful output measure alongside welfare indicators

options.label: E
options.text: A complete welfare indicator suitable for exclusive use

explanation: states that "GDP is a useful indicator of a nation's economic performance, but it has some limitations." The balanced view - GDP is useful but limited - is the standard AP position. GDP should not be dismissed, but its limitations (especially nonmarket transactions) must be recognized when interpreting it as a welfare measure.

prompt: Which of the following correctly lists examples of nonmarket transactions that are excluded from GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: Unpaid housework and volunteer services

options.label: B
options.text: Imports, transfers, and used-car sales

options.label: C
options.text: Debt interest, dividends, and capital gains

options.label: D
options.text: New housing, stock purchases, and bond sales

options.label: E
options.text: Foreign trade, tax revenue, and retained earnings

explanation: Unpaid housework (cooking, cleaning, childcare), volunteer services (tutoring, charity work), and subsistence farming (growing food for own consumption) are all classic examples of nonmarket transactions that produce genuine value but are excluded from GDP because they lack a recorded market price. This is the primary limitation cited in MEA-1.B.1.

prompt: GDP is a better indicator of economic ACTIVITY than of economic WELFARE. Which of the following best supports this distinction?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher output need not mean greater overall welfare

options.label: B
options.text: Price adjustment makes GDP a complete welfare measure

options.label: C
options.text: Output and welfare are identical at full employment

options.label: D
options.text: Output and welfare are identical at every employment level

options.label: E
options.text: GDP measures output only after adjusting for population

explanation: Economic "activity" is GDP's strength - it tracks how much is bought and sold in markets. "Welfare" is multidimensional and includes nonmarket production, environmental quality, distribution, leisure, health, and freedom - dimensions GDP doesn't capture. GDP can rise while welfare falls (e.g., after a disaster, from harmful goods, with rising inequality), illustrating the activity-welfare gap.

prompt: In which of the following situations would GDP most significantly UNDERSTATE actual economic well-being?

options.label: A
options.text: An economy with mostly recorded industrial production

options.label: B
options.text: An economy with government purchases equal to 30% of GDP

options.label: C
options.text: An economy exporting recorded goods at market prices

options.label: D
options.text: An economy with nearly all services formally purchased

options.label: E
options.text: An economy with substantial unrecorded production

explanation: GDP understates well-being most severely when large amounts of real production occur outside formal markets. An economy with extensive subsistence farming (nonmarket production) and a large underground cash economy has significant real output that is not captured in official GDP; the gap between measured GDP and actual economic activity is largest in such economies.

prompt: A student claims: "If real GDP rises, people must be better off." Which of the following GDP limitations would most directly challenge this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Defensive spending can increase without improving underlying well-being

options.label: B
options.text: GDP necessarily grows faster than population each year

options.label: C
options.text: GDP rises only when government purchases increase

options.label: D
options.text: GDP remains constant and cannot rise or fall

options.label: E
options.text: Real GDP necessarily grows whenever nominal prices rise

explanation: Even if GDP rises in real terms, the composition of that output matters. Spending on pollution cleanup, security systems, litigation costs, and harmful products all raise GDP without improving - and potentially reflecting a decline in - well-being; this makes the student's claim too simplistic and highlights the composition and defensive expenditure limitations of GDP.

prompt: Which of the following best explains why a country with high total GDP might still have many citizens living in poverty?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher total output necessarily means higher consumer prices

options.label: B
options.text: High-output economies necessarily have high poverty rates

options.label: C
options.text: Higher total output necessarily reduces workers’ real wages

options.label: D
options.text: Total output does not reveal who receives the income

options.label: E
options.text: All high-output economies exclude legal market transactions

explanation: Total GDP tells us the size of the economy's output, not how it is distributed. A country can have enormous total GDP while most of that income accrues to a tiny wealthy elite, leaving many citizens in poverty; the failure to capture income distribution is a fundamental limitation of GDP as a welfare indicator.

prompt: Country X has a GDP of $800 billion and a population of 40 million. Country Y has a GDP of $400 billion and a population of 10 million. Which country has the higher GDP per capita, and what does this reveal about a limitation of using total GDP for cross-country comparisons?

options.label: A
options.text: X $40,000; Y $20,000; output per person favors X

options.label: B
options.text: X $20,000; Y $40,000; output per person is equal

options.label: C
options.text: X $20,000; Y $40,000; total GDP obscures population differences

options.label: D
options.text: X $40,000; Y $40,000; output per person is equal

options.label: E
options.text: X $20,000; Y $20,000; output per person is equal

explanation: Country X GDP per capita = $800B ÷ 40M = $20,000; country Y GDP per capita = $400B ÷ 10M = $40,000. Despite Country Y having half the total GDP, its average citizen has access to twice as much output because the population is much smaller; this illustrates why total GDP is a poor cross-country measure of living standards - population size must be accounted for.

prompt: A country' government reports a 5% increase in GDP this year. An economist cautions that this figure may overstate improvement in well-being. She cites three factors: rising inequality, increasing pollution from industrial growth, and longer average work weeks. Evaluate each factor as a GDP limitation.

options.label: A
options.text: GDP already deducts inequality, pollution, and lost leisure

options.label: B
options.text: GDP deducts pollution costs but includes leisure benefits

options.label: C
options.text: GDP omits distribution, environmental damage, and leisure value

options.label: D
options.text: Greater inequality necessarily increases every household’s consumption

options.label: E
options.text: Only pollution matters; inequality and leisure have no welfare effects

explanation: All three are genuine GDP limitations: (1) GDP ignores income distribution - growth can accrue entirely to the wealthy while average citizens see no improvement. (2) Pollution costs (reduced health, degraded ecosystems) are not subtracted from GDP; (3) Longer working hours produce more output (raising GDP) but reduce leisure time, a genuine component of well-being; GDP growth of 5% that is accompanied by all three may significantly overstate welfare improvement.

prompt: Country A has high GDP per capita but also very high levels of air and water pollution. Country B has moderately lower GDP per capita but pristine environmental quality. A student concludes: "Country A is unambiguously better off." Evaluate this conclusion.

options.label: A
options.text: B can have higher welfare only with a larger population

options.label: B
options.text: A necessarily has higher welfare if healthcare is affordable

options.label: C
options.text: Environmental quality can outweigh output differences

options.label: D
options.text: Higher output per person proves A has higher welfare

options.label: E
options.text: Future cleanup spending proves A currently has higher welfare

explanation: GDP per capita measures average market output, not holistic well-being; environmental quality - clean air, clean water, biodiversity - directly affects health, life expectancy, and quality of life. A country with higher GDP per capita but severe pollution may have worse actual welfare outcomes than one with lower GDP but a healthy environment; this illustrates why GDP alone is insufficient for welfare comparisons.

prompt: An economist studies two countries with the same real GDP per capita of $25,000. In Country A, the Gini coefficient (a measure of inequality) is 0.25 (relatively equal). In Country B, it is 0.55 (highly unequal). What does this comparison reveal about a limitation of GDP per capita?

options.label: A
options.text: Average output completely describes both countries’ economic welfare

options.label: B
options.text: Equal output per person requires identical Gini coefficients

options.label: C
options.text: The Gini coefficient measures cross-country price differences

options.label: D
options.text: More equal income distribution necessarily lowers measured output

options.label: E
options.text: Equal average output can conceal greater inequality in B

explanation: GDP per capita is a mean (average) - it divides total output equally among the population regardless of actual distribution. In Country B with a Gini of 0.55, a large majority of citizens likely live on far less than $25,000 while a small wealthy class pulls the average up; the same GDP per capita can correspond to very different real welfare outcomes depending on income distribution.

prompt: A developing nation has a large informal economy where goods and services are exchanged in unrecorded transactions. An economist estimates that informal economic activity equals 30% of official GDP. Which statement best assesses the implications for GDP as an economic indicator?

options.label: A
options.text: Tax evasion necessarily overstates official GDP by 30%

options.label: B
options.text: Informal workers produce no economically valuable goods or services

options.label: C
options.text: Official GDP already contains every unreported transaction exactly

options.label: D
options.text: Unreported transactions cancel, leaving official GDP fully accurate

options.label: E
options.text: Missing production can distort measured output and international comparisons

explanation: If the informal economy is 30% of official GDP, then actual economic activity is roughly 30% larger than what official statistics capture. This systematic understatement distorts living standard comparisons (countries with large informal sectors appear artificially poor), skews growth rate calculations, and complicates policy analysis; the limitation is especially severe in many developing economies.

prompt: A country passes laws reducing the standard workweek from 48 to 40 hours, giving workers significantly more leisure time. Other things equal, this policy will likely

options.label: A
options.text: Leave GDP unchanged because leisure has a market price

options.label: B
options.text: Necessarily raise GDP by the government’s enforcement costs

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce output while potentially improving welfare through greater leisure

options.label: D
options.text: Necessarily raise GDP because fewer hours always improve productivity

options.label: E
options.text: Reduce output and welfare because leisure has no value

explanation: Reducing work hours decreases market production (other things equal), so measured GDP falls. However, workers now have more leisure time, which has real value to them - they can spend more time with family, pursue hobbies, rest, and so on; if workers value this leisure more than the forgone wages, their well-being may actually increase even as GDP decreases; this tension between GDP and well-being is a core limitation of GDP.

prompt: Two countries produce the same total GDP of $1 trillion. Country A produces mostly consumer goods (food, medicine, clothing, housing) and educational services. Country B produces mostly military weapons. A policymaker claims: "Both countries are equally well-off." Evaluate this claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Military output is entirely excluded from measured GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Equal population guarantees equal welfare at equal GDP

options.label: C
options.text: Trade necessarily equalizes welfare between both countries

options.label: D
options.text: Equal output need not provide equal civilian welfare

options.label: E
options.text: Equal GDP proves both countries have identical welfare

explanation: GDP does treat both equally in dollar terms - this is precisely the limitation the question targets. GDP's indifference to the composition of output means it cannot distinguish between production that directly improves well-being (food, medicine, education) and production that does not directly contribute to civilian welfare (military weapons); the policymaker's statement reflects how GDP is calculated, but also why GDP is an incomplete welfare measure.

prompt: An economy experiences a severe hurricane. In Year 1, the hurricane destroys $10 billion of infrastructure. In Year 2, $8 billion is spent rebuilding. How do these events affect measured GDP, and what limitation does this reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither destruction nor reconstruction enters measured GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Destruction subtracts $10B; rebuilding adds no new output

options.label: C
options.text: Destruction subtracts $10B; rebuilding adds $8B directly

options.label: D
options.text: Insurance adds $10B; reconstruction subtracts $8B output

options.label: E
options.text: Destruction is not directly deducted; rebuilding adds $8B output

explanation: Year 1: The hurricane destroys capital (infrastructure), but destruction itself is not a market transaction and does not appear in GDP; measured GDP does not fall due to the destruction. Year 2: The $8B rebuilding effort is economic output (construction services, materials), so GDP rises; GDP therefore appears to rise from hurricane reconstruction without accounting for the $10B of destruction; this "broken window" limitation means GDP can rise in the wake of disasters.

prompt: Previously unrecorded gambling becomes reliably measured after legalization. The volume of activity is unchanged. What happens to measured GDP when the previously omitted production is included?

options.label: A
options.text: New tax revenues are added directly to GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Regulatory spending is deducted directly from GDP

options.label: C
options.text: Existing output cannot enter measured GDP after legalization

options.label: D
options.text: Legal production is counted twice as income and expenditure

options.label: E
options.text: Better recording raises measured output without increasing underlying activity

explanation: Including previously omitted production raises measured GDP without creating additional underlying output. Legalization alone need not raise measured GDP: some illegal activity may already be estimated. The stated change in statistical coverage drives this result.

prompt: A country adopts a new measure as an illustrative "adjusted welfare indicator", which starts with GDP but adds nonmarket activities (volunteer work, household production) and subtracts costs of crime, pollution, and inequality. The indicator is lower than GDP for this country. What does this suggest about the limitations of GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: Every adjusted welfare indicator must equal conventional GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Welfare adjustments matter only above global average output

options.label: C
options.text: The adjustments identify welfare costs absent from conventional GDP

options.label: D
options.text: Market pricing makes GDP a complete welfare measure

options.label: E
options.text: A lower adjusted figure means conventional GDP understates welfare

explanation: If GPI < GDP for this country, it means the costs that GDP ignores (crime, pollution, inequality) exceed the value of nonmarket activities it omits (volunteer work, home production). In net terms, GDP overstates well-being for this country; GPI-type measures were developed precisely because economists recognized GDP's limitations as a welfare proxy.

prompt: Country A has GDP per capita of $18,000. Country B has GDP per capita of $22,000. However, Country A has cleaner air, lower crime rates, longer average life expectancy, and more equal income distribution. A student concludes that Country B has higher well-being. Evaluate this conclusion.

options.label: A
options.text: Income always outweighs every health and environmental consideration

options.label: B
options.text: PPP adjustment alone makes the welfare ranking definitive

options.label: C
options.text: A’s health and environmental advantages may offset B’s higher income

options.label: D
options.text: B’s higher income proves greater overall welfare

options.label: E
options.text: B’s future income necessarily resolves its current social problems

explanation: This scenario directly tests the multi-dimensional nature of well-being vs; GDP per capita. Country A's advantages - lower pollution (better health), lower crime (more personal safety), longer life expectancy, and more equal distribution - are all components of well-being that GDP does not capture; these could easily outweigh the $4,000 per capita income gap; the student's reliance on GDP per capita alone exemplifies the limitations of GDP as a welfare measure.

prompt: An economist says: "Any spending that occurs in markets should count in GDP, including money spent on treating opioid addiction, repairing car crash damage, and providing prison services." A critic argues this is a flaw in GDP. Who is more consistent with the standard critique of GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: Market production should be excluded if associated with harm

options.label: B
options.text: Counting remedial spending makes GDP a complete welfare measure

options.label: C
options.text: All government production must be excluded from GDP

options.label: D
options.text: Remedial spending enters GDP without deducting the underlying harm

options.label: E
options.text: GDP must measure only market spending that improves welfare

explanation: The critic's point is a well-known limitation: GDP does not distinguish between expenditures that reflect genuine improvements in well-being and "defensive" expenditures that merely offset problems or restore prior conditions. Addiction treatment, accident repair, and incarceration all add to GDP but reflect social dysfunction; an ideal welfare measure would net out these costs rather than counting them as progress.

prompt: A household that previously hired a housekeeper ($600/month) decides the primary caregiver will quit their part-time job to do the housekeeping themselves. What are the effects on measured GDP and actual economic activity?

options.label: A
options.text: Unpaid household cleaning is fully recorded in standard GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Paid cleaning output rises when the family replaces the housekeeper

options.label: C
options.text: Paid cleaning output rises while household production remains unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: Paid cleaning disappears from GDP when replaced by unpaid work

options.label: E
options.text: Every household market transaction disappears when cleaning becomes unpaid

explanation: Two effects: (1) The $600/month housekeeper payment is no longer recorded - GDP falls by $600/month; (2) The caregiver's part-time job income (consumer spending on goods bought with that income) may also be lost. Meanwhile, the house is equally clean; GDP decreases even though the same cleaning service is being produced - the nonmarket/market boundary creates an artificial reduction in measured GDP that does not reflect a real decline in output.

prompt: Economists sometimes argue that GDP growth in high-income countries is less informative about well-being than GDP growth in low-income countries. Why might this be the case?

options.label: A
options.text: Smaller total output automatically makes GDP a better welfare measure

options.label: B
options.text: Higher-income countries necessarily have higher inflation rates

options.label: C
options.text: Higher-income welfare depends exclusively on further output growth

options.label: D
options.text: Income can yield smaller welfare gains once basic needs are met

options.label: E
options.text: Higher income makes output a complete welfare measure

explanation: As basic needs are met, additional income may contribute less to well-being. Improvements in health, leisure, environmental quality, or income distribution can matter greatly while being incompletely reflected in GDP. Higher production therefore does not capture every improvement in welfare.

prompt: A country's economy becomes increasingly automated. Robots replace human workers in factories, dramatically increasing output (and GDP) while many workers lose jobs and income. Which limitations of GDP does this scenario highlight?

options.label: A
options.text: Factory automation necessarily reduces measured total output

options.label: B
options.text: Replacing humans with robots leaves output unchanged by definition

options.label: C
options.text: Higher market output proves every household’s welfare improved

options.label: D
options.text: Robots’ labor-force exclusion causes output to be understated

options.label: E
options.text: Higher output can coexist with unequal gains and lost job satisfaction

explanation: Rising automation can simultaneously increase GDP (more output per hour of capital) while worsening inequality (income shifts from labor to capital) and causing job displacement. GDP rises, but: (1) the income distribution limitation means GDP growth understates how unequally the gains are shared; (2) work provides non-monetary benefits (identity, social connection, purpose) that aren't in GDP; both limitations make GDP a poor guide to overall welfare in this transition.

prompt: A government announces it will begin counting the estimated value of household services (cooking, cleaning, childcare) in its national accounts. What effect would this have on measured GDP, and would it address the nonmarket transaction limitation?

options.label: A
options.text: Expanded coverage necessarily makes household services economically worthless

options.label: B
options.text: Measured output falls as unpaid services become recorded

options.label: C
options.text: Measured output stays unchanged because all housework already counts

options.label: D
options.text: Expanded household-service coverage raises recorded production

options.label: E
options.text: Recorded household services are deducted from measured output

explanation: Imputing values for household services (assigning estimated market prices to unpaid work) would raise measured GDP by adding previously omitted nonmarket production; this directly addresses the nonmarket transaction limitation. Note: Some countries already impute values for owner-occupied housing (homeowners are treated as renting to themselves), showing that statistical agencies can and do make such adjustments - though comprehensive household service imputation remains rare.

prompt: Country X has GDP growing at 4% per year. Its population is growing at 3% per year. A policymaker celebrates: "Our economy is growing fast." An economist responds that GDP per capita is the more relevant measure for living standards. Calculate approximate GDP per capita growth and evaluate the policymaker's optimism.

options.label: A
options.text: Per-person growth approximately 7%; optimism understates growth

options.label: B
options.text: Per-person growth approximately 1%; total growth overstates per-person gains

options.label: C
options.text: Per-person growth 3%; equal to population growth

options.label: D
options.text: Per-person growth −1%; population grows faster than output

options.label: E
options.text: Per-person growth 4%; population growth has no effect

explanation: Approximate GDP per capita growth ≈ GDP growth rate - population growth rate = 4% - 3% = 1%. The policymaker sees headline GDP growth and is encouraged, but most of that growth is simply supporting a larger population - average output per person is barely rising; this illustrates why GDP per capita is the relevant metric for living standards, and why ignoring population growth (a limitation of using total GDP alone) leads to unwarranted optimism.

prompt: Health outcomes (life expectancy, infant mortality, disease prevalence) are not captured in GDP. A public health expert argues that GDP growth in Country A does not necessarily indicate better health outcomes. Provide the most accurate assessment of this argument.

options.label: A
options.text: Health matters only if healthcare spending is excluded

options.label: B
options.text: Higher output necessarily produces better health outcomes

options.label: C
options.text: Output per person perfectly predicts health outcomes

options.label: D
options.text: Health matters only below $10,000 output per person

options.label: E
options.text: Healthcare spending does not directly measure health outcomes

explanation: GDP measures healthcare spending but not health outcomes. A country can spend enormous amounts on medical care for a sick, unhealthy population and have high healthcare-related GDP while its citizens live shorter, less healthy lives than another country with lower healthcare spending but better preventive care, nutrition, and environmental quality; health outcomes are a welfare dimension that GDP cannot directly capture.

prompt: A critic of using GDP as a welfare measure points out that countries with similar GDP per capita can have very different levels of happiness or life satisfaction (as measured by surveys). Which limitations of GDP does this observation most directly reflect?

options.label: A
options.text: Subjective well-being and nonmaterial life satisfaction

options.label: B
options.text: Survey data cannot contain any meaningful welfare information

options.label: C
options.text: High income necessarily eliminates every happiness difference

options.label: D
options.text: Equal average income necessarily implies equal happiness

options.label: E
options.text: Entertainment spending fully measures subjective happiness

explanation: Life satisfaction surveys consistently show that countries with similar GDP per capita can have significantly different self-reported happiness. This is because happiness depends on many factors beyond income: social trust, political freedom, personal relationships, work-life balance, meaning and purpose, and community belonging - none of which are market transactions captured by GDP; this highlights GDP's fundamental limitation as a welfare proxy.

prompt: Country A spends $50 billion on crime prevention, prisons, courts, and security systems. Country B has the same total GDP but spends only $20 billion on these items because it has far lower crime rates. Assuming everything else is identical, which country has better welfare, and what GDP limitation does this illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Government security purchases always improve welfare by their cost

options.label: B
options.text: Equal total GDP proves both have identical welfare

options.label: C
options.text: B has better welfare only with higher per-capita GDP

options.label: D
options.text: B needs less defensive spending, freeing resources for other uses

options.label: E
options.text: Higher security spending proves A has better welfare

explanation: The "defensive expenditure" limitation: Crime-prevention spending is counted positively in GDP even though it arises from a social problem. Country B's lower crime means its citizens are safer AND have $30B more available for goods that directly improve welfare; with equal total GDPs, Country B is better off - but this is not visible in the GDP figures; GDP fails to net out the costs of social dysfunction.

prompt: An economist says: "Comparing GDP across countries using current exchange rates can be misleading because the purchasing power of a dollar differs across countries." Which aspect of GDP's limitations does this statement highlight?

options.label: A
options.text: Exchange rates affect only net exports, never comparisons

options.label: B
options.text: Exchange-rate conversion always overstates developing-country incomes

options.label: C
options.text: PPP addresses international differences in purchasing power

options.label: D
options.text: Identical currencies guarantee identical purchasing power

options.label: E
options.text: Every GDP comparison already uses PPP prices

explanation: When comparing GDP across countries using market exchange rates, countries with lower price levels appear poorer than they really are because each dollar of local currency buys more locally than it would internationally. PPP adjustments account for price level differences across countries, giving a better sense of comparative purchasing power and living standards; this is a well-recognized limitation of simple exchange-rate-based GDP comparisons.

prompt: A nation increases spending on advertising by $200 billion. This raises measured GDP. Does more advertising spending indicate higher economic well-being? Explain using a GDP limitation.

options.label: A
options.text: Advertising expenditure need not equal its contribution to welfare

options.label: B
options.text: Advertising is subtracted from GDP because it changes preferences

options.label: C
options.text: Higher sales guarantee advertising improves welfare by its cost

options.label: D
options.text: Every market transaction increases welfare by its expenditure value

options.label: E
options.text: Advertising spending always increases welfare by its full cost

explanation: Advertising is counted as a service in GDP, but its welfare contribution is contested. Some advertising informs consumers (net positive), but much of it is persuasive in a zero-sum way - brand A's gain is brand B's loss; either way, GDP counts it identically with spending on food, medicine, or housing; GDP's inability to distinguish between types of services or assess their net social value is a genuine limitation.

prompt: A country shifts from manufacturing goods to providing services over two decades. GDP remains roughly constant in real terms. However, researchers note that many new service jobs involve shorter hours, better working conditions, and more autonomy. What does this suggest about GDP as a welfare measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Constant GDP proves working conditions and welfare are unchanged

options.label: B
options.text: Services are inherently less valuable than manufactured goods

options.label: C
options.text: Better working conditions can raise welfare at unchanged output

options.label: D
options.text: All services lack market prices and are excluded

options.label: E
options.text: GDP directly measures every improvement in workplace conditions

explanation: GDP measures the dollar value of output, not the conditions under which work is performed. If the same GDP is produced with more pleasant, flexible, and autonomous working conditions, workers are genuinely better off - but this improvement is invisible in GDP; work quality is a component of well-being that GDP systematically ignores, causing it to miss welfare improvements (or deteriorations) associated with changes in job characteristics.

prompt: A statistician observes that as a country becomes more developed, its informal economy typically shrinks relative to its formal (market) economy. What implication does this have for GDP comparisons between developed and developing countries?

options.label: A
options.text: Informality necessarily makes measured output exceed actual production

options.label: B
options.text: Market adjustment makes informal production automatically appear in records

options.label: C
options.text: Formalization can improve recording without new production

options.label: D
options.text: Formal economies exclude every officially recorded market transaction

options.label: E
options.text: Informal production is always perfectly captured in official statistics

explanation: When informal activity becomes formalized (businesses register, workers receive reported wages), it appears in GDP statistics even if no additional real production has occurred. Some GDP growth in developing countries therefore reflects formalization - moving from unmeasured to measured activity - rather than genuine output growth; this makes level comparisons between developed (mostly formal) and developing (partly informal) economies inherently tricky.

prompt: A country's GDP rises significantly following a large-scale deforestation effort that generates $30 billion in timber revenue. An environmental economist argues this GDP increase is misleading. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: Timber exports are subtracted as imports from measured GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Timber output does not directly deduct lost forest assets

options.label: C
options.text: Timber sales are always excluded as intermediate output

options.label: D
options.text: Timber royalties alone measure every environmental cost

options.label: E
options.text: GDP directly deducts all future losses when forests are cut

explanation: GDP treats the extraction of natural resources as income while ignoring the depletion of the natural capital stock. A forest generates ongoing, year-after-year ecosystem services - but cutting it down yields a one-time timber payment counted as positive GDP; the permanent loss of the forest and its ecosystem services is not subtracted. "Green GDP" or "adjusted net savings" concepts attempt to correct for this by treating resource depletion as a cost, not just income.

prompt: Using a supply-and-demand framework applied to the "market for well-being," an economist argues that GDP captures only the goods and services that have market prices, but well-being also includes "goods" with no market (clean air, public safety, social trust) and subtracts "bads" (pollution, inequality, crime) that GDP ignores. Which of the following best evaluates this framework?

options.label: A
options.text: Nonmarket welfare matters only when output is declining

options.label: B
options.text: All nonmarket welfare factors lack economic significance

options.label: C
options.text: Government purchases fully measure every public-good benefit

options.label: D
options.text: Economic analysis cannot address nonmarket welfare effects

options.label: E
options.text: Market output omits nonmarket benefits and external costs

explanation: The economist's framework correctly identifies that GDP captures well-being imperfectly in two directions: it omits non-market goods that add to welfare (clean air, social cohesion, volunteerism) and also fails to subtract market-generated bads (pollution, crime costs) that reduce welfare. A genuinely comprehensive welfare indicator would need adjustments in both directions - adding omitted positives and subtracting counted negatives that reduce net welfare.

prompt: A researcher compares two countries using the Human Development Index (HDI), which combines GNI per capita with life expectancy and education levels. Country A ranks higher on GDP per capita but lower on HDI than Country B. What does this reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: Different indicators cannot provide complementary information

options.label: B
options.text: Different rankings prove B has greater unrecorded production

options.label: C
options.text: HDI is a better direct measure of total output

options.label: D
options.text: Higher income does not guarantee better health and education

options.label: E
options.text: Different rankings prove a GDP measurement error

explanation: HDI combines life expectancy, education, and GNI per capita. GDP per capita measures domestic output per person and is an incomplete welfare indicator. Different rankings show that higher domestic output per person does not guarantee a higher overall human-development index; they do not establish a GDP error or prove a specific difference in unrecorded production.

prompt: A policymaker argues: "We should use GDP per capita to determine how to allocate foreign aid between Country X (GDP per capita $12,000) and Country Y (GDP per capita $8,000)." An economist objects that GDP per capita alone is insufficient. What other dimensions should be considered?

options.label: A
options.text: Identical currency and records eliminate every welfare difference

options.label: B
options.text: Distribution, health, education, and access to essential services

options.label: C
options.text: Income per person should be the exclusive aid criterion

options.label: D
options.text: Total output alone is preferable to per-person output

options.label: E
options.text: Income per person fully describes every aid need

explanation: GDP per capita provides a useful first-cut estimate of average income but misses: (1) within-country inequality (high average may mask deep poverty); (2) health, education, and institutional quality; (3) informal sector activity; and (4) access to basic services. A country with GDP per capita of $12,000 but extreme inequality, poor health, and bad governance may need more aid than one with $8,000 but equal distribution and functional institutions.

prompt: Technological improvements in smartphones have dramatically increased their functionality over time. A new smartphone in 2024 is far more powerful than one in 2014, yet the price has barely changed. If statistical quality adjustments are incomplete, how could this affect GDP's accuracy as a welfare measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer required devices necessarily make output growth overstated

options.label: B
options.text: Quality adjustments perfectly capture every improvement in every product

options.label: C
options.text: Incomplete quality adjustments can understate real consumer gains

options.label: D
options.text: Quality can never affect inflation-adjusted output measures

options.label: E
options.text: Improved phones necessarily make measured welfare too high

explanation: When product quality improves without a commensurate increase in price, GDP may understate real welfare gains. If you pay the same $800 for a phone that is dramatically better, your consumer surplus (the value received beyond price) increases - but GDP only records the $800 transaction; statistical agencies try to adjust for quality using hedonic pricing methods, but these adjustments are imperfect, potentially causing GDP to miss some real quality-of-life improvements.

prompt: Country A and Country B each have GDP per capita of $20,000. Country A's citizens work an average of 2,200 hours per year; Country B's citizens work an average of 1,600 hours per year. What does this comparison reveal about the limitations of GDP per capita?

options.label: A
options.text: B has more leisure at the same output per person

options.label: B
options.text: Longer hours prove greater output per hour in A

options.label: C
options.text: Hours worked cannot be analyzed as an economic variable

options.label: D
options.text: Equal output per person fully captures differences in leisure

options.label: E
options.text: More working hours necessarily mean greater overall welfare

explanation: GDP per capita divides total income by population without considering how many hours were worked to generate it. Country B produces the same per-capita output with 600 fewer annual work hours, implying: (1) higher labor productivity in Country B, and (2) more leisure time for Country B's citizens; leisure is a real welfare benefit invisible in GDP; country B's citizens are likely better off despite identical GDP per capita.

prompt: An economist proposes "Green GDP" — a version of GDP that subtracts the estimated cost of environmental damage and resource depletion from conventional GDP. In a heavily polluting economy, Green GDP would be significantly lower than conventional GDP. What does this proposal address?

options.label: A
options.text: Exclusion of all environmental regulatory purchases

options.label: B
options.text: Inclusion of unpaid household services in standard GDP

options.label: C
options.text: Failure to reveal differences in income distribution

options.label: D
options.text: Failure to adjust nominal GDP for inflation

options.label: E
options.text: Failure to deduct environmental damage and resource depletion

explanation: Conventional GDP counts pollution cleanup as positive output while not subtracting the pollution damage or natural resource depletion that necessitated it. Green GDP subtracts environmental costs (pollution damage, resource depletion) from conventional GDP, yielding a measure of output that is sustainable - net of environmental destruction; this directly targets the limitation that GDP ignores negative environmental externalities.

prompt: A country experiences a sharp rise in anxiety, depression, and stress-related illness following rapid industrialization, even as its GDP grows at 7% per year. Which limitations of GDP are most relevant here?

options.label: A
options.text: Distress is not directly deducted; treatment spending counts as output

options.label: B
options.text: GDP deducts mental-health costs from measured output

options.label: C
options.text: Healthcare expenditures fully measure mental-health outcomes

options.label: D
options.text: GDP necessarily falls whenever stress-related illness increases

options.label: E
options.text: Government healthcare services are excluded from measured output

explanation: Two GDP limitations interact here: (1) GDP does not directly measure mental health, happiness, or psychological well-being; rising anxiety and depression reduce quality of life in ways not visible in GDP. (2) The defensive expenditure problem: spending on mental healthcare treatment is counted as positive GDP output even though it arises from a social decline; GDP rises partly because of the problem, not despite it.

prompt: An economist notes that in Country Z, a large proportion of economic activity consists of barter — people exchanging goods and services directly without using money. How does this affect GDP measurement and the country's welfare picture?

options.label: A
options.text: Every barter transaction is automatically recorded without estimates

options.label: B
options.text: Barter is excluded because every barter transaction is illegal

options.label: C
options.text: Only agricultural barter is excluded from measured output

options.label: D
options.text: Avoiding tax automatically raises measured GDP for barter

options.label: E
options.text: Unrecorded barter may be missed despite producing countable output

explanation: Money payment is not required for production to count in GDP. Barter can be valued at comparable market prices, but unrecorded informal exchanges are difficult for statisticians to observe. The issue is incomplete coverage, not an automatic exclusion of all barter.

prompt: A country with very high GDP per capita has among the world's highest rates of incarceration. The costs of running prisons — staff salaries, facility construction, food — are all counted in GDP. Does this high GDP per capita accurately reflect the well-being of citizens?

options.label: A
options.text: No — incarceration reduces GDP because it removes workers from the labor force

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — high incarceration costs reflect strong rule of law, which supports economic activity

options.label: C
options.text: No; prison spending does not directly measure safety or well-being

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — GDP per capita fully accounts for all public services including prisons

options.label: E
options.text: GDP accurately reflects welfare here because prison spending is government output that society demands

explanation: High incarceration costs are a form of defensive expenditure: they arise from a social problem (high crime or punitive sentencing policies) and are counted as positive GDP without subtracting the underlying social cost. A society requiring enormous prison spending to manage a crime problem is not better off than one with low crime requiring minimal incarceration - yet GDP may rank them similarly or even rank the high-incarceration society higher due to the prison spending.

prompt: In comparing two equally sized developing economies, Country P has a large formal banking sector and extensive formal markets; Country Q has limited formal finance and relies heavily on informal credit and unrecorded trade. Other things equal, which country's GDP more accurately reflects its actual level of economic activity?

options.label: A
options.text: P's recorded markets make its production easier to measure

options.label: B
options.text: Country Q's GDP is more accurate because informal markets are more efficient

options.label: C
options.text: Both countries' GDPs are equally accurate because GDP is measured the same way everywhere

options.label: D
options.text: GDP accuracy is not affected by the degree of formality in an economy

options.label: E
options.text: Country Q's GDP is more accurate because informal markets avoid double-counting

explanation: GDP is constructed from recorded market transactions; the more economic activity passes through formal, measurable channels, the more completely GDP captures actual output. Country P, with formal banking and extensive market records, has most of its output captured in GDP; country Q, with widespread informal credit and unrecorded trade, has a larger fraction of real activity excluded from official GDP, making Country P's GDP a more complete measure of its economy.

prompt: A rapidly urbanizing country sees families moving from rural subsistence farms to cities where they buy food, pay rent, and purchase services. GDP rises sharply. However, the economist observes that some of this GDP growth reflects not an increase in production but a shift from nonmarket to market activity. Explain.

options.label: A
options.text: GDP rises solely because urban wages are higher than rural subsistence income

options.label: B
options.text: GDP is unaffected by urbanization because the food was always produced in the same quantity

options.label: C
options.text: Formalization may raise measured GDP without increasing underlying production

options.label: D
options.text: Urbanization reduces GDP because rural families were producing more efficiently on farms

options.label: E
options.text: GDP rises because government spending on urban infrastructure is counted in the national accounts

explanation: This is a classic example of the nonmarket transaction limitation in a dynamic context; subsistence food production was real but uncounted. As families move to cities and buy food in stores, the same nutritional value becomes a market transaction counted in GDP; the GDP growth overstates real output growth because it partly reflects measurement improvement (nonmarket → market) rather than a true increase in production.

prompt: A country's GDP grows by $500 billion in a year. Of that, $200 billion results from increased production of pollution-causing industries whose pollution imposes estimated damages of $300 billion on health and environment. What is the net welfare impact, and what does this reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: Net welfare is unchanged because pollution costs and production benefits always offset each other

options.label: B
options.text: Net welfare rises by $500 billion — GDP accurately captures all costs through market prices

options.label: C
options.text: Pollution creates a $100B net loss in the affected activities

options.label: D
options.text: Net welfare rises by $200 billion — the GDP contribution of the polluting industries

options.label: E
options.text: GDP overstates output by $300 billion — the cleanup costs that will be required in the future

explanation: The polluting industries contribute $200B to GDP but impose $300B of external damage costs on third parties (health costs, ecosystem damage). The net social value is $200B - $300B = -$100B: these industries make society worse off on net, even though they raise GDP; GDP counts their $200B of output without subtracting the $300B of damage - a direct illustration of the environmental externality limitation of GDP as a welfare measure.

prompt: A government report shows that real GDP per capita has risen 2% annually for 20 years in Country Z. A skeptic argues that life satisfaction surveys show no improvement in average well-being over the same period. Which explanation is most consistent with standard GDP limitations?

options.label: A
options.text: The surveys are unreliable; GDP is the only scientifically valid welfare measure

options.label: B
options.text: The skeptic's data must be wrong — rising real GDP per capita always improves well-being

options.label: C
options.text: Inequality, pollution, or lost leisure can offset rising average output

options.label: D
options.text: The skeptic is correct — GDP per capita must fall for life satisfaction to fall

options.label: E
options.text: Life satisfaction and GDP are positively correlated by definition, so rising GDP always raises satisfaction

explanation: The empirical finding that rising GDP can coincide with stagnant or falling life satisfaction is well-documented (the "Easterlin paradox" in some contexts). Multiple GDP limitations can explain this: rising inequality means most gains go to the wealthy; environmental degradation offsets income gains; longer work hours reduce leisure; social trust may have declined; and consumption goods may have become more defensive in nature; GDP's failure to capture these dimensions explains the divergence.

prompt: Country A has high GDP per capita but very low social mobility (children's economic outcomes are strongly tied to their parents'). Country B has lower GDP per capita but high social mobility. Which country's GDP better reflects future well-being?

options.label: A
options.text: Country A, because high GDP per capita enables children to inherit more wealth

options.label: B
options.text: Average current output omits mobility and the distribution of opportunity

options.label: C
options.text: Country B, because high social mobility always leads to higher future GDP

options.label: D
options.text: Both countries have equal well-being because GDP per capita is the definitive welfare measure

options.label: E
options.text: Country A, because GDP per capita directly measures current well-being, which always matters more than mobility

explanation: Social mobility - the ability of individuals to move up the economic ladder regardless of their origin - is a dimension of well-being, fairness, and future opportunity that GDP per capita does not capture. A society with high GDP per capita but rigid class stratification (low mobility) may offer less genuine opportunity to most citizens than one with lower current income but fluid mobility; GDP measures where the average person is, not how easily anyone can improve their position.

prompt: A critic says: "The fact that GDP can rise after a divorce (because two households now pay separately for services they shared) and after a car accident (due to auto repair spending) shows that GDP is fundamentally broken as a welfare measure." Is this criticism valid?

options.label: A
options.text: The criticism is valid only if the country has a GDP below the global median

options.label: B
options.text: These examples expose welfare limitations without invalidating GDP as an output measure

options.label: C
options.text: The criticism is invalid because divorce and accidents create real jobs and economic activity

options.label: D
options.text: The criticism is invalid — these events genuinely increase economic output and are correctly counted

options.label: E
options.text: The criticism is fully valid — GDP should never rise when a social negative occurs

explanation: The divorce-and-accident critique is a well-known illustration of GDP's limitations: it counts spending generated by misfortune as positive output. However, "fundamentally broken" overstates the case - GDP remains useful for tracking market output, business cycles, and growth trends; the nuanced AP position: GDP has real, significant limitations (including defensive expenditures), but it is still a useful and informative economic indicator, just not a complete welfare measure.

prompt: Country A has nominal GDP of $2 trillion, population of 50 million, a Gini coefficient of 0.60, an average of 55 work hours per week, severe urban air pollution, and a life expectancy of 62 years. Country B has nominal GDP of $1.5 trillion, population of 40 million, a Gini coefficient of 0.25, an average of 38 work hours per week, clean air, and a life expectancy of 80 years. Using a comprehensive welfare analysis, evaluate which country provides higher well-being to its typical citizen.

options.label: A
options.text: Both countries have equal well-being because their GDP per capita figures are similar

options.label: B
options.text: B's leisure, equality, environment, and longevity may offset its lower income

options.label: C
options.text: Country A — its higher total GDP proves it is wealthier

options.label: D
options.text: Country A — its GDP per capita ($40,000) exceeds Country B's ($37,500), making it unambiguously better off

options.label: E
options.text: Country A — it has higher productivity per worker, which is the best welfare measure

explanation: This multi-dimensional comparison uses the comprehensive GDP limitations framework: (1) Distribution: Country A's Gini of 0.60 means most citizens earn far less than $40,000 - the high average is driven by a wealthy elite. Country B's $37,500 is more broadly shared; (2) Leisure: 55 vs. 38 hours/week - Country B's citizens have 17 more hours of weekly leisure, a significant well-being component. (3) Environment: Severe vs. clean air - health, longevity, and quality of life differ massively; (4) Life expectancy: 62 vs. 80 years - 18 additional years of life in Country B; the $2,500 per capita income gap is easily overwhelmed by these dimensions.

prompt: An economist argues: "A comprehensive welfare measure would equal GDP minus defensive expenditures minus environmental degradation costs minus the value of increased inequality, plus the value of nonmarket production plus the value of leisure. In practice, this measure often grows more slowly than GDP in industrialized countries." Evaluate this argument and identify which GDP limitations each adjustment addresses.

options.label: A
options.text: The argument is valid but applies only to developing economies, not industrialized countries

options.label: B
